los.text: Describe the clinical features and examination findings in a patient with heart failure and how these can be used to formulate a differential diagnosis and outline initial management.
sessions: Student Case Presentation: patient with heart failure
los.html:
Symptoms
  • Breathlessness (exertional → at rest)
  • Orthopnoea (number of pillows)
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
  • Fatigue
  • ↓ exercise tolerance
  • Ankle swelling
  • Weight gain
  • Nocturnal cough (pink frothy sputum in acute pulmonary oedema)
  • Wheeze ("cardiac asthma")
  • Abdominal swelling/anorexia (right-sided: hepatic congestion, ascites)
  • Nocturia
  • Confusion (elderly).
Signs
  • Tachycardia
  • Irregular pulse (AF)
  • Low-volume pulse
  • Hypotension (advanced) or hypertension (cause)
  • Raised JVP
  • Positive hepatojugular reflux
  • Displaced apex (LV dilatation)
  • S3 gallop
  • Murmurs (MR functional; AS/MR as cause)
  • Bibasal fine crackles
  • Pleural effusions
  • Pitting peripheral/sacral oedema
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Ascites
  • Cachexia
  • Cool peripheries.
NYHA classesI (no limitation), II (symptoms on ordinary activity), III (on less than ordinary activity), IV (at rest).
Differential diagnosis of breathlessness + oedemaHF vs COPD/ILD, renal failure/nephrotic (proteinuria), liver disease (hypoalbuminaemia), drugs (amlodipine oedema), venous insufficiency, obesity/deconditioning, anaemia, PE, thyroid disease, pulmonary hypertension.
Initial management
  • Confirm with NT-proBNP → echo
  • Acute: sit up
  • O₂ if hypoxic
  • IV furosemide
  • ± GTN infusion (if SBP >110)
  • CPAP for pulmonary oedema
  • Treat precipitant (ACS, AF, infection, non-adherence, NSAIDs, uncontrolled HTN)
  • Chronic: diuretics for congestion, start disease-modifying drugs (LO 3, 7), daily weights, fluid/salt advice.

los.text: Explain the role of common investigations in the diagnosis and assessment of heart failure, and how results guide management.
sessions: Diagnosis and management of heart failure
los.html:
NT-proBNP(released from stretched ventricular myocytes)
  • NICE NG106 thresholds: >2000 ng/L → specialist assessment and echo within 2 weeks
  • 400–2000 → within 6 weeks
  • <400 makes HF unlikely (in untreated patients).
  • Raised also by: age >70, AF, LVH, ischaemia, CKD, sepsis, PE, COPD/pulmonary hypertension, diabetes, cirrhosis
  • Lowered by obesity (BMI >35), diuretics/ACEi/ARNI (sacubitril raises BNP but not NT-proBNP), Afro-Caribbean ethnicity.
Transthoracic echocardiogram(key test)
  • LVEF → classifies HFrEF (≤40%), HFmrEF (41–49%), HFpEF (≥50% with structural/diastolic abnormalities and ↑ natriuretic peptides)
  • LV size/wall thickness, regional wall motion (ischaemia), valve disease, diastolic function, RV function, pulmonary pressures, pericardial effusion.
  • Guides drug therapy (most proven drugs are for HFrEF) and device eligibility.
ECG
  • Almost always abnormal in HF (normal ECG makes HFrEF unlikely): AF
  • LVH
  • Q waves (previous MI)
  • LBBB (QRS duration ≥130–150 ms → CRT)
  • Bradyarrhythmias.
CXRCardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, alveolar oedema, effusions; excludes lung disease.
BloodsFBC (anaemia), U&E (baseline for diuretics/ACEi; CKD), LFTs, TFTs, HbA1c, lipids, iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation: iron deficiency → IV iron), urinalysis.
Further (cause)
  • Coronary angiography/CT coronary angiography (ischaemic cause)
  • Cardiac MRI (cardiomyopathies, myocarditis, infiltration, viability, scar)
  • Stress testing
  • Holter (arrhythmias)
  • Genetic testing (familial cardiomyopathy)
  • Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (transplant assessment).
Guide management
  • LVEF → drug choice and devices
  • Cause (ischaemia → revascularisation; valve → intervention; AF → rate/rhythm and anticoagulation)
  • Renal function/K⁺ → drug titration
  • Iron deficiency → IV iron.

los.text: Explain the mechanisms of action of drugs used to treat heart failure and how these relate to their clinical use and common side effects.
sessions: Pharmacology and therapeutics of heart failure
los.html:
Drug classExampleMechanismClinical useCommon side effects
ACE inhibitorsRamipril, lisinopril↓ Ang II → vasodilation (↓ afterload), ↓ aldosterone (↓ Na⁺/water retention), ↓ remodellingHFrEF: ↓ mortality and hospitalisationCough, hypotension, ↑K⁺, ↑ creatinine, angioedema
ARBsCandesartan, losartanAT1 receptor blockIf ACEi not toleratedAs ACEi (no cough)
ARNISacubitril/valsartan (Entresto)Neprilysin inhibitor (↑ natriuretic peptides: natriuresis, vasodilation) + ARBReplace ACEi/ARB in symptomatic HFrEF (PARADIGM-HF: ↓ mortality vs enalapril); stop ACEi 36 h beforeHypotension, ↑K⁺, renal impairment, angioedema
β-blockers (HF-licensed)Bisoprolol, carvedilol, nebivololBlock sympathetic overactivity → ↓ HR, ↓ arrhythmias, ↓ remodelling, ↑ diastolic filling timeHFrEF: ↓ mortality (~35%), ↓ sudden death; "start low, go slow"Fatigue, bradycardia, hypotension, initial worsening; caution in asthma
MRAsSpironolactone, eplerenoneAldosterone antagonism → ↓ fibrosis, Na⁺ retentionHFrEF (RALES/EMPHASIS)↑K⁺, ↑ creatinine, gynaecomastia (spironolactone)
SGLT2 inhibitorsDapagliflozin, empagliflozinGlycosuria/natriuresis, ↓ preload, metabolic and renal effectsHFrEF and HFpEF (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR): ↓ HF hospitalisation/CV death, regardless of diabetesGenital thrush, volume depletion, euglycaemic DKA (rare)
Loop diureticsFurosemide, bumetanideBlock NKCC2 → natriuresisSymptom relief of congestion (no mortality benefit)↓K⁺, ↓Na⁺, dehydration, AKI, gout, ototoxicity (high-dose IV)
IvabradineIf (funny) channel block → ↓ HRHFrEF in sinus rhythm HR ≥75 despite β-blockerVisual phosphenes, bradycardia
DigoxinNa⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition → ↑ contractility; vagal ↓ AV conductionAF rate control, symptomatic HFrEF (↓ admissions)Toxicity (nausea, visual (yellow), arrhythmias; ↑ with ↓K⁺, renal impairment)
Hydralazine + nitrateVasodilatorsBlack patients/ACEi-ARB intolerant (A-HeFT)Headache, lupus-like
IV ironFerric carboxymaltoseCorrects iron deficiencySymptoms, ↓ admissions
  • Avoid in HF: NSAIDs, non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) in HFrEF, pioglitazone, class I antiarrhythmics, dronedarone, saxagliptin.

los.text: Describe the overall management of heart failure, including non-pharmacological measures.
los.html:
Non-pharmacological measures
  • Education and self-management (recognise worsening: weight gain >2 kg in 3 days → contact HF nurse/increase diuretic)
  • Daily weights
  • Salt restriction (moderate)
  • Fluid restriction only if severe/hyponatraemic (1.5–2 L)
  • Cardiac rehabilitation/exercise (improves symptoms, QoL)
  • Smoking cessation
  • Alcohol reduction (abstinence in alcohol-related cardiomyopathy)
  • Weight management
  • Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID)
  • Treat comorbidities (sleep apnoea, diabetes, anaemia, depression)
  • HF specialist nurse follow-up
  • Telemonitoring
  • Driving (DVLA rules)
  • Palliative care when appropriate.
Devices
  • ICD (implantable cardioverter-defibrillator): prevents sudden cardiac death from VT/VF; secondary prevention (survived VT/VF arrest) or primary prevention if LVEF ≤35% despite ≥3 months optimal medical therapy (NYHA I–III), especially ischaemic.
  • CRT (cardiac resynchronisation therapy, biventricular pacing): for LVEF ≤35% + broad QRS (≥130–150 ms, especially LBBB) in sinus rhythm despite OMT → resynchronises LV contraction → ↓ symptoms, ↓ admissions, ↓ mortality. CRT-D combines with defibrillator.
  • Left ventricular assist device (LVAD): bridge to transplant or destination therapy in advanced HF.
  • Pacemakers for bradyarrhythmias (conduction disease); cardiac contractility modulation, baroreflex activation (selected).
Surgical/interventionalSee LO 8.
MDTCardiologist, HF nurse, GP, pharmacist, dietitian, physio, palliative care.

los.text: Explain how the pathophysiology of heart failure relates to its clinical presentation and treatment.
los.html:
Definition
  • The heart can't pump enough blood for the body's needs, or only by raising filling pressures.
  • Caused by a structural or functional cardiac abnormality.
Causes
  • Ischaemic heart disease (commonest in UK)
  • Hypertension
  • Valve disease (AS, MR)
  • Cardiomyopathies (dilated: genetic, alcohol, viral myocarditis, peripartum, chemotherapy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab); hypertrophic; restrictive (amyloid))
  • Arrhythmias (AF, tachycardia-induced)
  • Congenital
  • Pericardial (constriction)
  • High-output (thyrotoxicosis, anaemia, AV fistula, Paget's, beriberi).
Pathophysiology → presentation
  • ↓ cardiac output → compensatory neurohormonal activation: sympathetic (↑ HR, contractility, vasoconstriction), RAAS (Ang II vasoconstriction; aldosterone Na⁺/water retention), ADH (water retention → hyponatraemia), natriuretic peptides (counter-regulatory but overwhelmed). Initially supportive, chronically maladaptive → ↑ preload and afterload, myocardial remodelling (hypertrophy, fibrosis, apoptosis, dilatation), arrhythmias → vicious cycle.
  • Backward failure (congestion): ↑ LV filling pressure → ↑ pulmonary venous pressure → interstitial/alveolar pulmonary oedema → breathlessness, orthopnoea (redistribution of fluid when supine), PND, crackles; right-sided failure → ↑ systemic venous pressure → ↑JVP, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly, ascites.
  • Forward failure (low output): fatigue, cool peripheries, renal hypoperfusion (oliguria, ↑ creatinine), confusion, cachexia, hypotension.
HFrEF (systolic: ↓ contractility, dilated LV) vs HFpEF (diastolic: stiff, hypertrophied LV with impaired relaxation; elderly, women, hypertension, obesity, diabetes, AF).
Treatment logic
  • Block neurohormonal systems (ACEi/ARNI, β-blockers, MRAs) to reverse remodelling and improve survival
  • SGLT2i
  • Diuretics relieve congestion
  • Treat cause
  • Devices for dyssynchrony/arrhythmias.

los.text: Explain how changes in ventricular size influence wall stress and cardiac function in heart failure.
los.html:
Laplace's lawWall stress (σ) ∝ (P × r) / (2h) (P = intraventricular pressure, r = radius, h = wall thickness).
Ventricular dilatation(↑ r: volume overload, after MI, dilated cardiomyopathy)
  • ↑ wall stress
  • → ↑ myocardial O₂ demand (wall stress is a major determinant), ↓ efficiency (larger chamber needs more tension to generate the same pressure), stretch-induced further remodelling and myocyte slippage
  • → progressive dilatation, functional mitral regurgitation (annular dilatation, papillary muscle displacement)
  • → more volume overload
  • → spiral of decline
  • Ischaemia (↑ demand + ↓ subendocardial perfusion), arrhythmias (stretch, fibrosis).
Compensatory hypertrophy
  • Concentric (pressure overload: hypertension, AS): sarcomeres added in parallel → ↑ wall thickness (h) → normalises wall stress but ↓ compliance → diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF), ↑ O₂ demand, subendocardial ischaemia.
  • Eccentric (volume overload: MR, AR, post-MI): sarcomeres added in series → chamber dilatation (↑ r) with modest wall thickening → wall stress rises → eventually systolic dysfunction.
Frank–StarlingInitially ↑ preload (stretch) ↑ stroke volume, but in failing heart the curve is flattened and over-stretched ventricles gain little → congestion without output gain.
Therapeutic implications
  • Reduce preload (diuretics)
  • Reduce afterload (ACEi/ARNI, vasodilators)
  • Reverse remodelling (β-blockers, ACEi, MRA, SGLT2i, CRT) → ↓ LV size and wall stress
  • Improved EF ("reverse remodelling").

los.text: Describe the overall management of heart failure, including non-pharmacological measures and the role of different classes of drug therapy.
los.html:
• HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%) treatment ("four pillars"; NICE NG106/ESC 2021–23): start and up-titrate as tolerated (often simultaneously/rapid sequencing):
1ACEi (or ARNI sacubitril/valsartan, or ARB if intolerant).
2β-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, nebivolol).
3MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone).
4SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin).
Plus
  • Loop diuretic for congestion (adjust to euvolaemia; "dry weight")
  • IV iron if iron deficient
  • Ivabradine (sinus rhythm, HR ≥75)
  • Digoxin (AF or refractory symptoms)
  • Hydralazine + nitrate (selected)
  • Devices (ICD/CRT)
  • Revascularisation/valve intervention.
  • Monitoring: U&E (K⁺, creatinine) 1–2 weeks after starting/up-titrating ACEi/ARNI/MRA; BP, HR; weight; titrate to target doses.
HFmrEFConsider similar approach (SGLT2i, diuretics; others may help).
HFpEF
  • SGLT2 inhibitor (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER), diuretics for congestion, treat comorbidities (hypertension, AF, obesity, diabetes, CKD, ischaemia), exercise
  • MRA/ARNI may help some
  • GLP-1 RA (semaglutide) improves symptoms in obese HFpEF.
Acute decompensated HFIV loop diuretics, O₂/CPAP, nitrates (if BP adequate), treat precipitant, inotropes (dobutamine) or vasopressors in cardiogenic shock, continue β-blocker unless shocked.
  • Non-pharmacological measures (LO 4)
  • Advanced HF: transplant/LVAD assessment, palliative care (symptom control: opioids for breathlessness, diuretics; deactivating ICDs at end of life after discussion; advance care planning).

los.text: Understand the role of surgery in the optimal management of the heart failure patient.
sessions: Surgical aspects of managing heart failure
los.html:
Surgical options in HF
  • Coronary revascularisation (CABG): ischaemic cardiomyopathy with significant multivessel disease, especially with viable myocardium/angina (STICH trial: CABG + OMT ↓ long-term mortality vs OMT alone).
  • Valve surgery/intervention: aortic valve replacement (SAVR/TAVI) for severe AS (removes pressure overload; often dramatic improvement), mitral valve repair/replacement for primary MR; transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER/MitraClip) for secondary (functional) MR in selected patients (COAPT); tricuspid interventions.
  • Mechanical circulatory support: LVAD (continuous-flow pump from LV apex to aorta) as bridge to transplant, bridge to candidacy/recovery, or destination therapy; complications: bleeding, pump thrombosis, driveline infection, stroke, RV failure; temporary devices (Impella, ECMO, IABP) in cardiogenic shock.
  • Heart transplantation: gold standard for selected patients with end-stage HF (NYHA IV despite maximal therapy, VO₂ max <12–14 mL/kg/min, no contraindications: active malignancy, irreversible pulmonary hypertension, severe comorbidity, active substance misuse); ~50% survival ~12+ years; lifelong immunosuppression (rejection, infection, malignancy, cardiac allograft vasculopathy).
  • Others: surgical ventricular restoration (aneurysmectomy), congenital repairs, pericardiectomy (constrictive pericarditis), septal myectomy (HOCM).
Optimal managementHeart Team (cardiologist, cardiac surgeon, imaging, HF nurse) decision; operative risk (EuroSCORE II), frailty, patient goals.

los.text: Locate the tibiofibular joints and explain that the superior is a synovial joint whilst the inferior is fibrous, and that only slight movement occurs.
los.html:
Tibiofibular joints
  • Superior (proximal) tibiofibular joint: between head of fibula and lateral tibial condyle; plane synovial joint; slight gliding movement (accommodates ankle movements).
  • Inferior (distal) tibiofibular joint (syndesmosis): between distal fibula and fibular notch of tibia; fibrous joint held by anterior and posterior inferior tibiofibular ligaments, interosseous ligament, inferior transverse ligament; very little movement (slight widening in dorsiflexion as the wider anterior talus wedges into the mortise).
  • Interosseous membrane (middle radio-ulnar-like "joint"): connects shafts; muscle attachment; separates anterior and posterior compartments.
Clinical
  • Syndesmotic ("high ankle") sprains (external rotation injury; squeeze test), Weber C fractures disrupt syndesmosis (unstable → fixation with syndesmotic screw), Maisonneuve fracture (proximal fibular fracture + syndesmosis/medial ankle injury)
  • Common peroneal nerve near fibular head.

los.text: Identify the (superficial and deep) muscles of the calf.
los.html:
Superficial posterior compartment
  • Gastrocnemius: two heads from femoral condyles (medial and lateral) → Achilles (calcaneal) tendon → calcaneus; plantarflexes ankle, flexes knee.
  • Soleus: from posterior tibia (soleal line) and fibula → Achilles tendon; plantarflexion (postural; important calf venous pump: soleal sinuses).
  • Plantaris: lateral supracondylar line of femur → long thin tendon → calcaneus (weak; tendon used for grafts).
  • Innervation: tibial nerve (S1–S2).
Deep posterior compartment
  • Popliteus: lateral femoral condyle → posterior tibia; "unlocks" the knee (laterally rotates femur on tibia).
  • Tibialis posterior: interosseous membrane, tibia, fibula → navicular tuberosity + other tarsals/metatarsals; inverts and plantarflexes, supports medial longitudinal arch (dysfunction → adult-acquired flatfoot).
  • Flexor digitorum longus: posterior tibia → distal phalanges 2–5; flexes toes.
  • Flexor hallucis longus: posterior fibula → distal phalanx of hallux; flexes big toe, push-off.
  • Innervation: tibial nerve (L4–S3); tendons pass behind the medial malleolus ("Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry": Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery, Vein, tibial Nerve, flexor Hallucis longus) through the tarsal tunnel under the flexor retinaculum.
ClinicalAchilles rupture (Simmonds'/Thompson squeeze test), calf DVT, compartment syndrome.

los.text: Label a diagram of the fascial compartments of the lower limb, particularly in the context of blood vessels and nerves.
los.html:
• Leg compartments (separated by interosseous membrane, anterior and posterior intermuscular septa and transverse intermuscular septum, enclosed by crural (deep) fascia):
CompartmentMusclesNerveArtery
AnteriorTibialis anterior, EHL, EDL, fibularis (peroneus) tertiusDeep fibular (peroneal) nerveAnterior tibial artery
LateralFibularis (peroneus) longus and brevisSuperficial fibular nervePerforating branches of fibular artery (no main artery)
Superficial posteriorGastrocnemius, soleus, plantarisTibial nerveSural branches (popliteal), posterior tibial
Deep posteriorPopliteus, tibialis posterior, FDL, FHLTibial nervePosterior tibial and fibular (peroneal) arteries
Thigh compartmentsAnterior (quadriceps, sartorius; femoral nerve; femoral artery), medial (adductors, gracilis; obturator nerve; profunda/obturator), posterior (hamstrings; sciatic nerve; perforating branches of profunda).
Diagram
  • Cross-section of mid-leg: tibia anteromedial, fibula lateral, interosseous membrane between them
  • Anterior compartment in front of membrane
  • Lateral compartment around fibula
  • Posterior compartment divided by transverse septum into superficial and deep.

los.text: Describe the fascial compartments enclosing the major muscle groups and explain the functional importance of these compartments and their contents in relation to compartment syndromes
los.html:
Fascial compartments
  • Muscle groups enclosed by unyielding deep fascia and bone
  • Each with shared function, nerve and blood supply
  • Functional advantages: efficient muscle contraction, venous return (calf muscle pump works because fascia is tight), containment of infection/haemorrhage.
Compartment syndrome
  • ↑ pressure within a closed compartment (from bleeding/oedema: fractures (especially tibial shaft), crush injury, reperfusion after ischaemia, burns (circumferential eschar), tight casts/bandages, prolonged immobilisation (drug overdose), exertion)
  • → pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure
  • → muscle and nerve ischaemia
  • → necrosis within ~6 h
  • → Volkmann's ischaemic contracture, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, infection, amputation.
Features
  • Pain out of proportion to injury
  • Pain on passive stretch of muscles in the compartment (earliest/most sensitive)
  • Tense/swollen compartment
  • Paraesthesia (nerve in compartment: e.g. 1st web space numbness = deep peroneal in anterior compartment syndrome)
  • Weakness/paralysis (late)
  • Pulses usually present (pulselessness is very late/arterial injury).
DiagnosisClinical; compartment pressure monitoring (absolute >30 mmHg or ΔP (diastolic BP − compartment pressure) <30 mmHg).
Management
  • Surgical emergency: remove casts/dressings, limb at heart level (not elevated), maintain BP, urgent fasciotomy (two-incision four-compartment fasciotomy of leg), debridement, delayed closure
  • Monitor for rhabdomyolysis (CK, renal function).
Chronic exertional compartment syndromeAthletes; pain with exercise relieved by rest.

los.text: Identify the bones of the ankle and foot on models and radiographs, and the ligaments stabilising the ankle joint
los.html:
Bones of ankle and foot
  • Tarsals (7): talus (body articulates with tibia/fibula in ankle mortise; head with navicular; no muscle attachments; retrograde blood supply → AVN after neck fractures), calcaneus (heel; sustentaculum tali supports talus), navicular, cuboid, medial, intermediate, lateral cuneiforms.
  • Metatarsals (5) (1st thickest; 5th base tuberosity: fibularis brevis), phalanges (14); sesamoids under 1st MTP.
Ankle (talocrural) joint
  • Synovial hinge joint (mortise: tibial plafond + medial malleolus + lateral malleolus (fibula) around talar dome)
  • Dorsiflexion/plantarflexion
  • Most stable in dorsiflexion (wider anterior talus wedged).
Ligaments
  • Medial (deltoid) ligament: strong, fan-shaped from medial malleolus to navicular, talus and calcaneus (sustentaculum); resists eversion; often avulses medial malleolus rather than tearing.
  • Lateral ligament complex (weaker): anterior talofibular (ATFL) (most commonly injured), calcaneofibular (CFL), posterior talofibular (PTFL) (strongest).
  • Syndesmotic ligaments (inferior tibiofibular).
Radiographs
  • AP/mortise and lateral ankle (malleoli, talar dome, joint space symmetry ~4 mm, syndesmosis), foot AP/oblique/lateral (tarsals, metatarsals, Lisfranc alignment, 5th metatarsal base, calcaneus: Böhler's angle).
  • Ottawa ankle rules for X-ray: bone tenderness at posterior edge/tip of either malleolus
  • Base of 5th metatarsal
  • Navicular
  • or inability to weight-bear 4 steps.

los.text: Recognise the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg, their innervation and blood supply.
los.html:
MuscleAttachmentsAction
Tibialis anteriorLateral tibia (upper ½), interosseous membrane → medial cuneiform + base of 1st metatarsalDorsiflexion, inversion; supports medial arch
Extensor hallucis longusMiddle fibula, interosseous membrane → distal phalanx of halluxExtends big toe, dorsiflexes
Extensor digitorum longusLateral tibial condyle, fibula → middle/distal phalanges 2–5Extends toes, dorsiflexes
Fibularis (peroneus) tertiusDistal fibula → base of 5th metatarsalDorsiflexion, eversion
InnervationDeep fibular (peroneal) nerve (L4–L5) (branch of common fibular nerve after it winds around fibular neck).
Blood supplyAnterior tibial artery (passes through interosseous membrane; continues as dorsalis pedis).
Clinical
  • Foot drop (common peroneal/deep peroneal palsy, L5 radiculopathy) → high-stepping gait
  • Anterior compartment syndrome
  • Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome)
  • Test: walking on heels, resisted dorsiflexion (L4), big toe extension (L5).

los.text: Explain the factors involved in the stability of the ankle joint, particularly the lateral ligaments, and explain the injury in 'sprain'.
los.html:
• Ankle stability factors:
    • Bony: mortise (malleoli grip the talus) → most stable in dorsiflexion (wider anterior talar dome); less stable in plantarflexion (narrower posterior talus) → most sprains occur in plantarflexion + inversion.
    • Ligamentous: medial deltoid (strong), lateral complex (ATFL, CFL, PTFL: weaker), syndesmosis.
    • Muscular/dynamic: fibularis longus and brevis (evertors protect against inversion), tibialis anterior/posterior, proprioception.
    • Capsule, tendons crossing joint.
Lateral ligamentAttachmentsInjury
ATFLAnterolateral malleolus → talar neck; taut in plantarflexionFirst and most commonly torn
CFLTip of malleolus → lateral calcaneus (crosses ankle and subtalar joints)More severe injuries
PTFLMalleolar fossa → posterior talus (strongest)Rarely injured
"Sprain"
  • Inversion injury in plantarflexion → stretching/tearing of the lateral ligaments (ATFL ± CFL).
  • Grades: I (stretch), II (partial tear, some laxity), III (complete rupture, instability: anterior drawer/talar tilt positive).
  • Swelling and bruising anterolateral, tenderness over ATFL.
Management
  • PRICE (protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation), analgesia, early weight-bearing and functional rehabilitation (proprioception/balance training, peroneal strengthening), brace for severe
  • X-ray if Ottawa rules positive
  • Complications: chronic instability, recurrent sprains, osteochondral talar dome lesions, missed fractures (5th metatarsal base, lateral talar process, anterior calcaneal process), syndesmotic injury.

los.text: Describe the arches of the foot and their importance, and explain how they are maintained by ligaments and muscles.
los.html:
ArchBonesNotes
Medial longitudinalCalcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms, medial 3 metatarsalsHighest; keystone = head of talus
Lateral longitudinalCalcaneus, cuboid, lateral 2 metatarsalsLow; rests on ground when standing
TransverseCuneiforms, cuboid, metatarsal bases
ImportanceShock absorption (spring-like), weight distribution (heel and metatarsal heads), adapt to uneven ground, rigid lever for propulsion (windlass mechanism), protect plantar nerves/vessels.
Maintenance
  • Bony shape (wedge-shaped bones; keystone).
  • Ligaments (static): plantar calcaneonavicular ("spring") ligament (supports head of talus: medial arch), long and short plantar ligaments (lateral arch), plantar aponeurosis (tie beam; windlass mechanism: dorsiflexion of toes tightens it, raising arch), interosseous ligaments.
  • Muscles (dynamic): tibialis posterior (main dynamic support of medial arch), tibialis anterior, fibularis longus (crosses sole: supports transverse and lateral arches; "stirrup" with tibialis anterior), FHL, FDL, intrinsic foot muscles.
ClinicalPes planus (flat foot) (flexible: normal in children; acquired: tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction, RA, Charcot), pes cavus (high arch: neurological: Charcot–Marie–Tooth, Friedreich's), plantar fasciitis.

los.text: Describe the movements of inversion and eversion at the subtalar joint, the muscles responsible, their innervations and main attachments
los.html:
• Subtalar (talocalcaneal) joint (+ talocalcaneonavicular joint): allows inversion (sole faces medially) and eversion (sole faces laterally), important for walking on uneven ground.
MovementMusclesNerveMain attachments
InversionTibialis posterior (main), tibialis anterior (with dorsiflexion), FDL, FHLTibial nerve (L4–L5); deep fibular (TA)TP → navicular tuberosity + plantar tarsals/metatarsals; TA → medial cuneiform + 1st metatarsal base
EversionFibularis (peroneus) longus, fibularis brevis, fibularis tertiusSuperficial fibular nerve (L5–S1); deep fibular (tertius)
  • FL → crosses sole in groove of cuboid → medial cuneiform + 1st metatarsal base
  • FB → tuberosity of 5th metatarsal base (avulsion fracture with inversion)
  • Tertius → 5th metatarsal dorsum
  • Clinical: common peroneal palsy → loss of eversion + dorsiflexion (inversion preserved)
    • L5 radiculopathy → weak inversion too
    • inversion injuries → lateral ligament sprain or fibularis brevis avulsion of 5th metatarsal base
    • tibialis posterior dysfunction → flat foot, weak inversion (can't do single-leg heel raise).

los.text: Trace the paths of the medial plantar artery and nerve and identify the structures they supply.
los.html:
Medial plantar artery
  • Smaller terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery (divides deep to abductor hallucis under flexor retinaculum)
  • → runs forward along the medial side of the sole between abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis
  • → supplies muscles of medial sole (abductor hallucis, FDB), skin of medial sole, and contributes to digital arteries of big toe
  • Superficial and deep branches
  • Anastomoses with plantar arch.
Medial plantar nerve
  • Larger terminal branch of the tibial nerve (in tarsal tunnel)
  • → accompanies artery
  • → supplies "LAFF" muscles: Lumbrical 1, Abductor hallucis, Flexor digitorum brevis, Flexor hallucis brevis
  • Sensory to medial ⅔ of sole and plantar surface of medial 3½ toes (like median nerve in hand).
ClinicalTarsal tunnel syndrome (tibial nerve compression behind medial malleolus) → burning/numbness of sole; jogger's foot (medial plantar nerve entrapment).

los.text: Trace the paths of the lateral plantar artery and nerve and identify the structures they supply.
los.html:
Lateral plantar artery
  • Larger terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery
  • → runs laterally and forwards between flexor digitorum brevis and quadratus plantae
  • → at base of 5th metatarsal turns medially to form the deep plantar arch (completed by the deep plantar branch of dorsalis pedis between 1st and 2nd metatarsals)
  • → plantar metatarsal arteries
  • → digital arteries
  • Supplies lateral sole muscles and most toes.
Lateral plantar nerve
  • Smaller terminal branch of tibial nerve
  • → accompanies artery between FDB and quadratus plantae
  • → superficial branch (sensory to lateral ⅓ of sole and lateral 1½ toes; flexor digiti minimi brevis, interossei of 4th space) and deep branch (with plantar arch: interossei, lumbricals 2–4, adductor hallucis)
  • Also quadratus plantae and abductor digiti minimi.
  • Supplies most intrinsic muscles of the foot (like ulnar nerve in hand).
Clinical
  • Dual blood supply (dorsalis pedis + posterior tibial via plantar arch) provides collateral flow
  • Diabetic neuropathy affects intrinsic muscles (claw toes, high plantar pressures → ulcers).

los.text: Identify the plantar aponeurosis, which helps stabilise the foot medially.
los.html:
Plantar aponeurosis (fascia)
  • Thick, strong band of deep fascia in the sole: from the medial tubercle of the calcaneus → divides into five slips inserting into the fibrous flexor sheaths and plantar plates of the toes (and skin)
  • Central part thickest, with medial and lateral parts.
Functions
  • Supports the longitudinal arches (especially medial) as a tie-beam/bowstring
  • Windlass mechanism (toe dorsiflexion during push-off winds the aponeurosis around metatarsal heads → shortens it → raises the arch and makes the foot a rigid lever)
  • Protects deeper plantar structures (vessels, nerves, tendons)
  • Origin for intrinsic muscles (FDB).
ConditionFeaturesManagement
Plantar fasciitis (commonest heel pain)Pain at medial calcaneal tubercle, worst on first steps in the morning; risk: obesity, standing, running, flat/high arches, tight AchillesStretching, insoles, analgesia, steroid injection, shockwave
Plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose)Nodules; associated with Dupuytren's
RuptureAfter steroid injections

los.text: Identify the muscles of the sole of the foot.
los.html:
• Four layers of the sole (superficial → deep):
LayerMuscles
1stAbductor hallucis (MPN), flexor digitorum brevis (MPN), abductor digiti minimi (LPN)
2ndQuadratus plantae (LPN) (corrects oblique pull of FDL), lumbricals (1: MPN; 2–4: LPN) + tendons of FDL and FHL
3rdFlexor hallucis brevis (MPN), adductor hallucis (oblique + transverse heads; LPN), flexor digiti minimi brevis (LPN)
4thPlantar interossei (3: adduct toes: "PAD"), dorsal interossei (4: abduct: "DAB") (LPN) + tendons of tibialis posterior and fibularis longus
DorsumExtensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis (deep fibular nerve).
FunctionsSupport arches, stabilise toes, fine adjustments during gait and balance, toe flexion/abduction/adduction.
Innervation summaryMedial plantar nerve → LAFF (lumbrical 1, abductor hallucis, FDB, FHB); lateral plantar nerve → all others.
Clinical
  • Intrinsic minus foot in neuropathy (diabetes, Charcot–Marie–Tooth) → claw toes, prominent metatarsal heads → ulcers
  • Morton's neuroma (interdigital nerve between 3rd/4th metatarsals).
